steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on turning multi-view 2D images into stylized 3D scenes made of vectorized 3D strokes. It should cover why current 2D/3D style transfer and NeRF stylization fall short, how painting with strokes motivates our approach, what the method does, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Style transfer: from 2D images to 3D scenes and NeRF, and its limits
2. Stroke-based painting vs. pixel/voxel manipulation
3. Our method: differentiable vectorized 3D stroke representation
4. Evaluation summary
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Style transfer -> 3D / NeRF
- artistic style image creation: used to need skill + time; revolutionized by neural style transfer
- methods separate, manipulate, merge content and style
- 3D harder: complex geometries + appearance traits; CNN methods not readily adaptable to 3D
- NeRF (3D implicit representation) popular: fully differentiable, easy to optimize
- NeRF stylization: separate NeRF training + style transfer, then integrate style transfer loss from multiple views
- still independent manipulation of content and style
- problem: only color changed, density/geometry unchanged -> no geometric changes

2. Strokes vs. pixels/voxels
- 2D/3D style transfer manipulates pixels or voxels
- traditional art: brushstrokes, randomness in brushes, materials, colors; time-consuming, skill-intensive
- automation: image generation with vectorized strokes (position, color, size, direction), optimized to match target images
- 3D painting tools, e.g. Google's Tilt Brush: VR/AR, various brushes, virtual spaces
- automated stroke-based 3D art generation relatively unexplored

3. Our method
- 2D images with known poses -> stylized 3D scenes with vectorized 3D strokes
- distinct geometric + appearance styles; emulates stroke-by-stroke painting of human artists
- vector-based -> render at any resolution
- range of 3D stroke styles; style and semantic losses for more intricate stylizations/generations
- core: differentiable vectorized 3D scene representation; differs from NeRF; parameterized 3D strokes synthesize 2D images at different viewpoints
- direct optimization of stroke parameters by gradient descent; no greedy search / reinforcement learning prediction as in earlier stroke-based image synthesis
- analyze gradient behaviors; stroke initialization + update scheme to avoid sub-optimal initialization / local minima

4. Evaluation
- multi-view datasets, real-world + synthetic images
- high-quality artistic 3D renderings; global visual fidelity, local color accuracy, perspective consistency

5. Contributions
- method: multi-view 2D images -> stylized 3D scenes; 3D strokes from basic primitives + spline curves; parameters learned by gradient descent
- initialization scheme for stroke parameters; addresses flat gradients
- various 3D stroke styles; geometry + appearance stylizations like human painters

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Creating images in an artistic style used to be something that needed a lot of skill and time, but neural network-based Style Transfer techniques have revolutionized it. Usually these methods separate the content and the style of the images, manipulate them, and then merge them to get an artistic effect. Doing the same for 3D scenes is challenging, however, because of the complex geometries and appearance traits, and the traditional convolutional neural network (CNN) methods cannot readily be adapted to 3D spaces. Recently 3D implicit scene representations have become popular, in particular Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), because they are fully differentiable and easy to optimize. The efforts to apply artistic styles to NeRF often train the NeRF and do the style transfer separately, and then integrate a style transfer loss from multiple views. So the basic approach is still to manipulate content and style independently. But the existing NeRF stylization techniques only change the color, and the density, and so the geometry, stays unchanged, which means the stylizations lack geometric changes.

Style transfer methods in 2D and 3D mostly manipulate pixels or voxels to get artistic effects. This is different from traditional art, where artists use brushstrokes and there is a degree of randomness in the brushes, the materials and the colors. The traditional approach takes a lot of time and skill. To automate it, research has looked at generating images with vectorized strokes, which are defined by position, color, size and direction and are optimized to match target images. There are also 3D painting tools like Google’s Tilt Brush that use VR/AR to create art scenes with various brushes in virtual spaces. However, automated stroke-based 3D art generation is still relatively unexplored.

- our method: 2D images with known poses -> stylized 3D scenes via vectorized 3D strokes; distinct geometric + appearance styles; emulates stroke-by-stroke painting of human artists
- vector-based -> any resolution; range of stroke styles; style + semantic losses for intricate stylizations/generations
- core: differentiable vectorized 3D scene representation, unlike NeRF uses parameterized 3D strokes to synthesize 2D images at different viewpoints
- gradient descent directly on stroke parameters (no greedy search / RL prediction as in earlier stroke-based image synthesis)
- gradient behavior analysis -> stroke initialization + update scheme, avoids sub-optimal init / local minima
- evaluation: multi-view datasets of real-world + synthetic images; high-quality artistic 3D renderings, global visual fidelity, local color accuracy, perspective consistency
- contributions: (1) multi-view 2D -> stylized 3D with 3D strokes from basic primitives + spline curves, learned by gradient descent; (2) initialization scheme against flat gradients; (3) various stroke styles, geometry + appearance stylizations like human painters

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Creating images in an artistic style used to be something that needed a lot of skill and time, but neural network-based Style Transfer techniques have revolutionized it. Usually these methods separate the content and the style of the images, manipulate them, and then merge them to get an artistic effect. Doing the same for 3D scenes is challenging, however, because of the complex geometries and appearance traits, and the traditional convolutional neural network (CNN) methods cannot readily be adapted to 3D spaces. Recently 3D implicit scene representations have become popular, in particular Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), because they are fully differentiable and easy to optimize. The efforts to apply artistic styles to NeRF often train the NeRF and do the style transfer separately, and then integrate a style transfer loss from multiple views. So the basic approach is still to manipulate content and style independently. But the existing NeRF stylization techniques only change the color, and the density, and so the geometry, stays unchanged, which means the stylizations lack geometric changes.

Style transfer methods in 2D and 3D mostly manipulate pixels or voxels to get artistic effects. This is different from traditional art, where artists use brushstrokes and there is a degree of randomness in the brushes, the materials and the colors. The traditional approach takes a lot of time and skill. To automate it, research has looked at generating images with vectorized strokes, which are defined by position, color, size and direction and are optimized to match target images. There are also 3D painting tools like Google’s Tilt Brush that use VR/AR to create art scenes with various brushes in virtual spaces. However, automated stroke-based 3D art generation is still relatively unexplored.

In this work we present a new technique that transforms 2D images with known poses into stylized 3D scenes using vectorized 3D strokes. Our approach recreates 3D scenes with distinct geometric and appearance styles, and it emulates the stroke-by-stroke painting process that human artists use. Because the system is vector-based, it can render at any resolution we want. It supports a range of 3D stroke styles, and with style and semantic losses it also supports more intricate stylizations and generations. At the core of the method is a vectorized 3D scene representation that is differentiable. It is different from NeRF in that it uses parameterized 3D strokes to synthesize 2D images at different viewpoints. Since the representation is differentiable, we can optimize the stroke parameters directly with gradient descent, so we don't need the greedy-search-based or reinforcement learning-based prediction methods used before in stroke-based image synthesis. We also analyze how the gradients behave in our stroke-based 3D representation, and we introduce a scheme for stroke initialization and update that avoids sub-optimal initialization, where optimization is difficult because of local minima.

We evaluated the method on multi-view datasets of real-world and synthetic images. The experiments show that it creates high-quality artistic renderings of 3D scenes, keeping both global visual fidelity and local color accuracy while also keeping perspective consistency. Our contributions are:

- We propose a new method to translate multi-view 2D images into stylized 3D scenes using 3D strokes based on basic primitives and spline curves, and their parameters can be learned with gradient descent.

- We present a new initialization scheme for the parameters of our stroke-based representation to deal with flat gradients during optimization.

- Our method supports various 3D stroke styles and can be used for sophisticated geometry and appearance stylizations like the ones human painters create.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Artistic style image creation, historically requiring significant skill and time, has been revolutionized by neural network-based Style Transfer techniques [1,2]. These methods usually separate, manipulate, and merge the content and style of images to create an artistic effect. Extending this to 3D scenes, however, is challenging because of complex geometries and appearance traits [3], and traditional convolutional neural network (CNN) methods [4] are not readily adaptable to 3D spaces. Recently, 3D implicit scene representations, particularly Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), have become popular since they are fully differentiable and easy to optimize. Efforts to apply artistic styles to NeRF [5,6,7] often involve separate NeRF training and style transfer, followed by integrating a style transfer loss from multiple views [8,9,10]. The fundamental approach is still the independent manipulation of content and style. Nevertheless, existing NeRF stylization techniques only alter color, leaving the density, and consequently the geometry, unchanged, so the resulting stylizations lack geometric changes.

Style transfer methods in 2D and 3D primarily manipulate pixels or voxels to achieve artistic effects, unlike traditional art where artists use brushstrokes and a degree of randomness in brushes, materials, and colors. This traditional approach is time-consuming and skill-intensive. To automate it, research has explored image generation with vectorized strokes [11], defined by position, color, size, and direction and optimized to match target images. 3D painting tools like Google’s Tilt Brush [12] use VR/AR to create art scenes with various brushes in virtual spaces. However, automated stroke-based 3D art generation remains relatively unexplored.

In this work, we present a novel technique for transforming 2D images with known poses into stylized 3D scenes using vectorized 3D strokes. Our approach recreates 3D scenes with distinct geometric and appearance styles, emulating the stroke-by-stroke painting process of human artists. The vector-based nature of our system allows rendering at any desired resolution. It accommodates a range of 3D stroke styles and supports more intricate stylizations and generations through style and semantic losses. The core of our method is a differentiable, vectorized 3D scene representation which, unlike NeRF, uses parameterized 3D strokes to synthesize 2D images at different viewpoints. This differentiable representation allows stroke parameters to be optimized directly via gradient descent, sidestepping the greedy-search-based or reinforcement learning-based prediction methods previously used in stroke-based image synthesis. Furthermore, we analyze the gradient behaviors of our stroke-based 3D representation and introduce a stroke initialization and update scheme that avoids sub-optimal initialization, where optimization is difficult due to local minima.

We evaluated our method on multi-view datasets of real-world and synthetic images. Our experiments demonstrate that it effectively creates high-quality artistic 3D scene renderings, maintaining both global visual fidelity and local color accuracy while ensuring perspective consistency. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- We propose a novel method to translate multi-view 2D images into stylized 3D scenes using 3D strokes based on basic primitives and spline curves, whose parameters can be learned through gradient descent.

- We present a novel initialization scheme for the parameters of our stroke-based representation that addresses flat gradients during optimization.

- Our method supports various 3D stroke styles and can be applied for sophisticated geometry and appearance stylizations similar to those created by human painters.
